newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia wraps up disarmament, political problems loom.
newsitem.headline: Liberia wraps up disarmament, political problems loom.

text.p: As the disarming of Liberia's civil war guerrillas entered a final phase on Friday, plans for a peaceful transition through elections ran into unexpected problems over the political framework for the polls.
U.N. officials said over 2,000 more guerrillas had turned in their weapons during a one-week extension of a voluntary disarmament period to midnight on Friday.

Latest U.N. figures showed a total of just over 20,000 guerrillas had now disarmed. The ECOMOG West African peacekeeping force whose figures are more comprehensive said a week ago about 23,000 or 71 percent had disarmed.
"Everybody would have reason to be pleased with the disarmament process," an international official said.

But diplomats and election experts said Liberia's peace process could be in difficulty again if a regional ministerial meeting in Monrovia next week does not resolve important issues that could imperil elections set for next May.
"The problem is that there is no political framework defining who should run elections or how they should be conducted," said a foreign election expert in Monrovia.

The critical issues are the composition of the electoral commission, revision of sections of the constitution regarding elections, and the question where Liberia's teeming population of refugees in neighbouring countries should vote.

Chief warlord Charles Taylor who launched civil war in December 1989 lambasted the United Nations on Thursday for its proposals for sitting three international representatives on the electoral commission.
"I am concerned about the sovereignty and dignity of this nation," Taylor told a news conference.
He also rejects U.N. proposals, still to be presented officially to the country's interim ruling council, on revising sections of Liberia's 1985 constitution regarding elections.

"The strange thing is that Taylor and other key presidential contenders will be disqualified under the constitution's 10-year residency clause if such sections are not revised," an international election adviser said.
Election experts surprised by Taylor's argument pointed to successful elections in South Africa and Mozambique where international officials were on the electoral commission.
Liberia has had an electoral commission since 1994 but its members are representatives of armed factions responsible for seven years of civil war in the West African nations.

Many ordinary Liberians say the commission is not credible and Western donors are not expected to fund the elections unless there is an independent commission on the ground. An alliance of seven political parties on Friday published a statement demanding an independent electoral commission.
Officials said Liberia's problem was caused by the terms of last August's regional accord which set a rigid poll timetable without first defining the type of elections to be held.
Taylor and fellow warlord Alhaji Kromah are meanwhile preparing to resign from the ruling council on February 28 in readiness to contest elections as the accord requires.

"If Taylor resigns on assumption that there will be elections and there are none because of the unresolved problems then there is prospect for confusion," one official said. "He will be angry, and he should be. They should have thought of these problems before asking people to resign."
